H1: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across all SKUs

hypothesis.title: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across all SKUs
hypothesis.explanation: The code uses a single module-level `asyncio.Lock()` (`_inventory_lock`) for every call to `inventory.reserve()`, regardless of SKU. With 500 concurrent users and ~187 req/s throughput, only one reservation can execute its database transaction at a time. The measured p99 ~760-820 ms is almost entirely queueing delay behind this lock.
supporting_evidence: app/inventory.py: `_inventory_lock = asyncio.Lock()` is global, acquired before any DB work
Baseline p99 760-820 ms vs target <100 ms (8x gap)
Throughput ~187 req/s implies critical section ~5.3 ms; p50 680 ms implies ~675 ms average wait
missing_evidence: Direct measurement of `inventory.lock_wait` and `inventory.lock_held` span percentiles

proposed_experiment.rationale: If the global lock is the dominant bottleneck, the in-process span `inventory.lock_wait` will show p99 in the hundreds of milliseconds (comparable to total request p99), while `inventory.lock_held` will be small (single-digit ms). If the lock is not the bottleneck, `lock_wait` p99 will be low (<10 ms) and the time will appear in `lock_held` or downstream DB spans.

predictions.if_supported: >= 500 ms at 500 users (comparable to http POST /inventory/reserve p99)
<= 20 ms at 500 users (just the DB transaction time)

predictions.observation: app_spans['http POST /inventory/reserve'].p99_ms vs sum of lock_wait + lock_held p99
predictions.if_supported: http p99 ≈ lock_wait p99 + lock_held p99 (within 20%)
predictions.if_refuted: http p99 significantly exceeds lock_wait + lock_held p99

hypothesis.title: Database connection pool too small for effective concurrency once app lock is removed
hypothesis.explanation: The pool is configured with min=5, max=20 (via DB_POOL_MIN_SIZE/MAX_SIZE). With the global lock in place, only one connection is used at a time, masking pool exhaustion. If H1 is true and the lock is the primary bottleneck, removing it would expose pool contention at 500 concurrent users because 20 connections cannot serve 500 parallel requestors.
supporting_evidence: Baseline shows only 187 req/s with 500 users; db CPU only 14-16% (idle)
Pool sizing is a common bottleneck when application-level serialization is removed
contradicting_evidence: Current db CPU is low, suggesting DB is not saturated
With global lock, pool usage is serialized so current data cannot confirm
missing_evidence: db.pool_acquire span percentiles under current load

proposed_experiment.rationale: Even with the global lock, we can measure `db.pool_acquire` latency and `db_activity.active_connections`. If the pool is already a latent bottleneck, `db.pool_acquire` p99 will be elevated (>50 ms) and `db_activity.active_connections.max` will approach 20 even though throughput is low. If the pool is adequate for current serialized load, `db.pool_acquire` p99 will be very low (<5 ms) and max active connections will be 1.

predictions.if_supported: >= 50 ms at 500 users (pool contention visible even with app lock)

predictions.if_refuted: <= 2 at 500 users (only 1 used due to app lock)

events.message: H3: PostgreSQL row-level lock contention on hot SKUs

hypothesis.title: PostgreSQL row-level lock contention on hot SKUs
hypothesis.explanation: Even without the application lock, concurrent reservations for the same SKU will serialize on PostgreSQL's row-level locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is not used in reserve, but UPDATE takes a row lock). If the load test (load/reserve.js) concentrates traffic on a small subset of the 1000 SKUs, database lock waits will dominate latency.
supporting_evidence: app/inventory.py: UPDATE products SET stock = ... WHERE sku = $1 takes row lock
Schema has 1000 SKUs but load test may not use them uniformly
db_activity.wait_events could reveal 'lock' wait event types
contradicting_evidence: Current db CPU only 14-16%, suggesting low DB contention
With global app lock, DB row locks are never contended (single thread)
missing_evidence: Load test SKU distribution (load/reserve.js not provided)

proposed_experiment.rationale: Measure `db_activity.wait_events` and `db.transaction` span. If row-lock contention is significant even under the app lock (unlikely but possible if lock is released between statements — it isn't), we'd see 'lock' wait events. More realistically, this hypothesis is about post-fix behavior, but we can check if the current workload *would* contend by examining SKU access pattern via `db_activity` and the `db.select_stock`/`db.update_stock` spans. If the load test hammers few SKUs, `db.select_stock` for those SKUs will show higher latency variance.

key_observations: At 500 concurrent users: http POST /inventory/reserve p99 = 771.4 ms; inventory.lock_wait p99 = 766.0 ms (99.3% of total latency); inventory.lock_held p99 = 6.8 ms
Sum of lock_wait p99 + lock_held p99 = 772.8 ms, matching http p99 (771.4 ms) within 0.2% — well inside the 20% prediction band
lock_wait p99 (766 ms) far exceeds the >=500 ms threshold for support; lock_held p99 (6.8 ms) is far below the <=20 ms threshold for support
At 100 concurrent users: lock_wait p99 = 6.9 ms, lock_held p99 = 7.2 ms, http p99 = 13.1 ms — sum (14.1 ms) ≈ http p99 (13.1 ms), consistent with low-contention baseline
conclusion.explanation: All three falsifiable predictions are confirmed by the measurements. The global asyncio.Lock serializes every reservation: at 500 concurrent users, 99.3% of the p99 latency is spent waiting for the lock (766 ms of 771 ms), while the critical section (lock_held) takes only ~7 ms. The http p99 equals the sum of lock_wait + lock_held p99 within measurement noise, confirming the lock queue is the dominant bottleneck.

events.message: Root cause: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across all SKUs

per-sku-asyncio-lock: Replace the single global asyncio.Lock with a per-SKU lock dictionary (defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)). This allows concurrent reservations for different SKUs to proceed in parallel while still serializing reservations for the same SKU in the application layer. The lock is held only for the duration of the database transaction (lock_held ~7ms p99), so contention is limited to same-SKU traffic.

This allows concurrent reservations for different SKUs to proceed in parallel while still serializing reservations for the same SKU in the application layer. The lock is held only for the duration of the database transaction (lock_held ~7ms p99), so contention is limited to same-SKU traffic.
candidate.expected_effect: At 500 concurrent users with uniform SKU distribution across 1000 SKUs, lock_wait p99 should drop from ~766ms to near zero (only same-SKU collisions queue). HTTP p99 should fall from ~770ms to ~15-20ms (lock_held + DB + network), well under the 100ms SLO. Throughput should increase proportionally.
candidate.risks: Memory growth if SKU space is unbounded (fixed at 1000 SKUs in seed data, so acceptable). Still serializes same-SKU reservations at application level, which is correct but could become a bottleneck if a single hot SKU receives extreme traffic. Lock dictionary never shrinks; long-running processes with dynamic SKUs could leak.

events.message: db-select-for-update: Remove the application-level asyncio.Lock entirely and rely on PostgreSQL's row-level locking via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside the database transaction. This lets the database serialize only conflicting SKUs (same row) while allowing full parallelism across different SKUs. The transaction holds the row lock only for the few milliseconds of the UPDATE/INSERTs (current lock_held p99 ~7ms).

candidate.strategy: Remove the application-level asyncio.Lock entirely and rely on PostgreSQL's row-level locking via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside the database transaction. This lets the database serialize only conflicting SKUs (same row) while allowing full parallelism across different SKUs. The transaction holds the row lock only for the few milliseconds of the UPDATE/INSERTs (current lock_held p99 ~7ms).
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates lock_wait entirely (0ms). HTTP p99 becomes lock_held p99 (~7ms) + DB overhead, targeting ~15-20ms p99 at 500 concurrent users — well under 100ms SLO. Throughput scales with database capacity, not application lock contention. Best architectural fit for a stateless service.
candidate.risks: Longer database transaction hold time (row lock held for entire transaction), but current lock_held p99 is only 6.8ms so impact is minimal. Requires correct transaction isolation (READ COMMITTED default works). If transaction logic expands significantly, row lock duration could become a contention point for hot SKUs — but that's correct behavior (database-level serialization of same-row updates).

events.message: optimistic-version-retry: Add a `version` column to the products table for optimistic concurrency control. Reservations read stock and version, then attempt an UPDATE with `WHERE version = old_version`. If the UPDATE affects 0 rows (concurrent modification), retry with exponential backoff (max 3 attempts). This eliminates all locking — application and database row locks — maximizing throughput. Only same-SKU conflicts cause retries.

candidate.expected_effect: Zero lock_wait, zero row-lock hold time. At 500 concurrent users with uniform SKU distribution, retries are rare (<1% for same-SKU collisions). HTTP p99 targets ~10-15ms (single DB round-trip + retries). Throughput limited only by database write capacity. Best horizontal scalability for high-contention workloads.
candidate.risks: Schema change required (add version column). Retry storms possible under extreme single-SKU contention (mitigated by exponential backoff and max attempts). Must ensure idempotency of reservation insert (unique constraint on reservation not needed; each attempt generates new reservation_id). Correctness depends on UPDATE's WHERE clause matching exactly one row — verified by checking rowcount. More complex logic increases bug surface area.
